title: Subprocessor Encryption & Access Evidence Exhibit — template
content:
Purpose:

This exhibit is intended to be attached to third-party processing agreements (DPA/SSA) to capture technical and evidentiary requirements relating to encryption, cryptographic key custody, and access proofing for subprocessors that will process or host sensitive customer data on behalf of Redwood Inference.

Scope and applicability:

- Applies to any subprocessor storing, transmitting, or decrypting customer prompt/response data, embeddings, or logs where the subprocessor has access to plaintext or decryption capabilities.
- Not required for purely pseudonymous telemetry where no meaningful reconstruction of customer content is possible — but should be evaluated case-by-case.

Definitions (brief):
- Customer Data: data provided by or generated for Redwood customers that is covered by a DPA
- Key Custody Model: who controls cryptographic key material (Redwood, customer, or subprocessor)
- Proofing Artifacts / Access Evidence: auditable artifacts demonstrating when, by whom, and how keys or decrypted data were accessed

High-level requirements (contract language examples included later):

1) Encryption in transit and at rest
- All Customer Data in transit must use TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites (AEAD preferred).
- Data at rest must be encrypted using AES-256-GCM or equivalent authenticated encryption.
- Where block storage snapshots/backups exist, they must be encrypted with separate keys from production volumes.

2) Key management and custody options (pick per engagement)
- Option A — Customer-managed keys (CMEK/CSEK): Customer or Redwood retains key control in a KMS/HSM that the subprocessor cannot export. Subprocessor may request decryption operations via API but cannot retrieve raw key material.
- Option B — Redwood-managed keys (BYOK to Redwood-managed KMS): Redwood owns keys in its cloud KMS; subprocessor has limited (non-exportable) key access scoped to the specific tenant.
- Option C — Subprocessor-managed keys: allowed only with strong compensating controls and prior security approval. (We prefer A/B.)

Key lifecycle expectations:
- Rotation cadence: rotation at least annually; high-sensitivity workloads may require rotation every 90 days.
- Destruction: keys tied to terminated contracts must be rotated/retired and evidence of destruction provided within 30 days of contract termination.
- Backup keys: key backups must be encrypted and access controlled; backup key access must be logged.

3) Hardware-backed KMS/HSM requirements
- If HSMs are used, they must be FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or equivalent in production.
- Subprocessor shall provide HSM vendor/family and firmware versions upon request.

4) Access control and human access to plaintext
- Principle of least privilege for ops and support staff. No standing access to decrypted customer data.
- Any break-glass or emergency access must be time-limited, pre-authorized per incident process, and fully logged.

5) Evidence and audit artifacts (access proofing) — minimum set
- KMS audit logs showing key usage events (Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign) with timestamp, principal ID, request origin IP, and request ID.
- System logs correlating KMS key use to VMs/containers/process IDs and a request trace ID that can be used to reconstruct the operation.
- Administrative console login records for users who can request decryption, including MFA evidence and session duration.
- Snapshot of IAM roles/policies in force at time of access.
- Copies of relevant support tickets/PRs with redacted content showing approval for elevated access (when applicable).

Evidence retention and delivery:
- Logs and audit artifacts must be retained for at least 1 year for production workloads (longer retention negotiable per customer).
- On customer request or as part of scheduled attestation, subprocessor will provide time-bounded extracts of the above artifacts within 15 business days.
- Where redaction is necessary for multi-tenant visibility, subprocessor must provide a procedure and reproducible method to show that redaction did not omit access-relevant metadata.

6) Attestation and periodic evidence refresh
- Quarterly self-attestation: subprocessor provides signed attestations that key custody and access controls remain as contracted, along with a small sample of redacted audit artifacts.
- Annual SOC/ISO/other third-party report supplemented with an encryption-specific bridge letter that calls out key custody model and how decryption access is controlled.

7) Onsite or remote audit rights
- Redwood reserves the right to perform remote evidence reviews and, for high-risk subprocessors, an onsite audit annually.
- Audit scoping and notice: Redwood will provide at least 10 business days notice for remote evidence reviews and 30 days for onsite audits.
- If subpoena / legal hold prevents delivery of certain logs, subprocessor must provide an explanation and alternative evidence promptly.

8) Incident response and key compromise
- Subprocessor must notify Redwood within 24 hours of any confirmed or reasonably suspected key compromise or unauthorized decryption.
- Must provide a mitigation plan, affected customer list, and forensic artifacts within 72 hours.
- If keys are compromised, subprocessor must support re-encryption, re-keying, and customer notification as required by Redwood’s DPA obligations.

9) Termination and return/destruction of keys & data
- Upon contract termination, subprocessor must: (a) cease processing, (b) securely erase plaintext data and ephemeral keys within agreed SLA (suggest 30–45 days), and (c) either return or cryptographically destroy key material and provide signed proof of destruction.

10) Minimum technical controls checklist (for onboarding)
- TLS endpoints with mTLS where possible
- KMS audit logs exported to an immutable storage location (read-only access by Redwood)
- IAM policies scoped to least privileges, with no shared accounts
- MFA for all administrative access
- Separated production and non-production key namespaces
- Backup key encryption and separate key rotation schedule

Sample contract clause (boilerplate for exhibit):

"Subprocessor shall ensure that all Customer Data is encrypted in transit and at rest using industry-standard cryptography. The parties agree that the Key Custody Model for the Services shall be [choose: Customer-managed / Redwood-managed / Subprocessor-managed]. Subprocessor shall retain auditable logs for all decryption operations and shall provide evidentiary extracts upon Redwood's request within fifteen (15) business days. Subprocessor shall notify Redwood within twenty-four (24) hours of any confirmed or suspected compromise of keys or unauthorized access to encrypted Customer Data and shall cooperate in remediation and customer notification at Subprocessor's expense if the compromise results in a Redwood DPA obligation to notify customers."

Negotiation playbook / redlines to expect (notes to SEs and legal):
- Vendors often push back on CMEK for multi-tenant shared SaaS. If they refuse CMEK, require strict attestation cadence, shorter retention of plaintext logs, and more frequent independent audits.
- Subprocessors want longer windows for log extraction (30–45 days) — push back to 15 for production incident response.
- HSM firmware/versions are often considered proprietary; accept summary disclosures but insist on FIPS-level and CVE remediation commitment.

Practical evidence examples (how to package):
- Provide KMS export slice: CSV of key usage events for the requested date range (redact ciphertext content).
- Provide IAM snapshot: current IAM role JSON + human-readable summary of role-to-principal mapping.
- Provide session metadata: support-ticket reference + requestor ID + time window + request justification.

Open items / TODOs for this template:

- Insert exact URL for attestation upload endpoint and agreed log exchange format.
- Add standard language for multi-cloud HSM equivalence testing.

Appendix A — Example evidence extract format (suggested columns):
- event_time, key_id, operation, principal_id, source_ip, request_id, resource_id, related_ticket_id

Appendix B — Example attestation wording (quarterly):

"Subprocessor attests that during the period [start]—[end], cryptographic key custody and access controls for Customer Data processed under Agreement [X] remained materially consistent with the Key Custody Model specified herein. Subprocessor further attests that no unauthorized decryption of Customer Data was identified during the period, except as noted in the attached exception log."

Notes to internal reviewers:
- This is intended as an exhibit / annex to the DPA, not a replacement for the DPA.
- Keep the template modular so teams can select CMEK vs Redwood-managed vs Subprocessor-managed sections.
- Tagging: include an index number that matches our contract tracker (see linked JIRA).
